title: Panel: Agentic AI in Capital Markets

segments.text: BRADLEY OLSON: Good break?
Everybody caffeinated?
Ready for some amazing insights?
I hope so.
We have a great group gathered here today.
My name is Brad Olson.
I'm the deputy Bureau chief at the Wall Street
Journal for technology.
And I'd love to actually allow these panelists to introduce
themselves.
And I've asked each of them to think--
have a response ready for what I call a starter question.
I think one of my favorite things
to do when we talk to people in AI
or in the AI race is to ask a little bit about what's
a wow moment they've experienced recently,
or even a moment where they might have been disappointed
by the performance of an AI model
or whatever their expectations were.
So I'd love to have everyone introduce themselves,
and if you could answer either side
of that question when you introduce yourself,
if you had a recent wow moment, or even some way in which maybe
what you thought would work with I
didn't live up to expectations.
Do you want to start?
JEFF WECKER: Oh, sure.
Sure.
So hi, everybody.
I want to thank the sponsors for inviting me.
My name is Jeff Wecker.
I run engineering for an investment management firm
called Two sigma.
Before that, I was a partner and the first chief data
officer for Goldman Sachs.
And before that, I was at Bridgewater Associates
and renovated their investment engine.
I can keep going, but I'm an old guy.
So there's a lot of before that as well.
So we'll stop there.
Do you want to--
do you want my answer for your question now?
BRADLEY OLSON: I think I'd love to.
It's a nice conversation starter.
JEFF WECKER: So amazing things, and I'm
embarrassed to say that a few years back,
I tried to use one of the LLMs for parenting advice.
And it was terrible, just absolutely terrible.
And I've tried it more recently.
And I actually got some pretty impressive results,
which I don't know if the LLMs have gotten better
or I got a lot worse, but very impressive, anyway.
BRADLEY OLSON: Very cool.
JEN ALLUM: Hi, I'm Jen Allum.
I'm one of the co-heads for one of the AI teams at DE Shaw.
And something that I found delightful recently,
perhaps not revelatory in usage, is having
AI be an executive coach.
I hope I'm not alone in this room
as being the only one with growth areas.
But it's delightful if there's something you're working on--
DE Shaw is very known for precise communication.
So it's an area I want to get better at.
And it's both wonderful for timely, actionable insight,
qualitative and quantitative, as long
as you give it the right context.
And I'm getting a ton of value out of it.
So I love that about it at the moment.
BRADLEY OLSON: Wonderful.
ALI NAZARI: I'll go next.
My name is Ali Nazari.
I run deep learning research team at Susquehanna.
Before that, I had my own startup.
It was actually deep learning hedge fund as well.
And before that, I was an information theorist.
I guess it's so easy to be excited
about entire evolution of AI and machine
learning AI and then agent systems in the past few years,
particularly last year.
What I want to take is actually disappointment.
A few weeks ago, I was--
maybe a month ago, I was trying to work on a research problem.
I asked one of these frontier AI models to help me,
think about it.
And it came up with something super exciting, super amazing,
came up with about 30 different plausible solutions.
Each of those ideas if I wanted to do myself,
it would probably take me months, if not quarters.
Then I realized actually the hardest part didn't disappear.
It just moved.
Now I found myself, instead of just
trying to come up with ideas to generate idea,
I was trying to figure out which of these ideas that
gave me worth my time.
And that's the reminder to me that all
of these bottlenecks, all of these challenges,
they don't just disappear.
They just move.
LI DENG: Yeah, my name is Li Deng.
I spent about 18 years at Microsoft.
And then I joined Citadel.
And now currently with Vatic Investments.
So before Microsoft, I was in academia.
At that time, I started doing neural network.
It never worked.
And even the first 10 years at Microsoft,
I turn everything, all my machine learning tools
into Bayesian networks, deep generative model,
but not done by neural network, but
by the standard statistical method.
And the result is just slow in our work on voice recognition
and translation of spoken language processing.
And the wow moment for me is started in 2010
when I first got the opportunity to look at a neural network.
Actually, it was inspired by Geoffrey Hinton.
Later on, he got a Nobel Prize.
And the first two or three experiments
that we tried already just shoot down the error rate
by about one third to one half.
And I immediately say, throw out all other tools.
Just embrace deep neural network.
We built very, at that time, up to about 13
or 14 layers in as early as 2010.
I was reminiscing with Jennifer earlier today.
At that time, most of the people at Microsoft
wouldn't believe that.
That was my big point.
And then the second wow moment for me
was when ChatGPT came out.
The first time I was trying ChatGPT about three years ago,
I just thought that something must go wrong.
That's exactly what many people said during my speech
recognition time at Microsoft.
They said, oh, you probably mixed training and test
data right.
Now for ChatGPT, we actually were
able to use that as the product.
So nothing could be wrong because it's real testing.
And then it took me--
I have to get back.
At that time, I was already in Wall Street there.
I have to get my previous team member who used to report to me.
He actually, at that time was leading the reasoning team
at Google.
And he had to explain to me that there
are certain kinds of decoding techniques
that is different than the traditional machine learning.
And then that made me immediately
realize that, wow, that's real.
But now when agentic AI came out,
there was a small amount of wow moment.
Actually, not just do pattern recognition, pattern matching,
the kind of traditional machine learning tasks,
but it actually can do the reasoning,
but also it can put things together.
It actually does knowledge management.
And that part really wowed me.
I'll stop right here.
BRADLEY OLSON: I think we've all had that experience where
there are a series of those moments for all of us.
One of the things that I wanted to ask,
because I imagine many of you are here
today to hear from people in finance and Wall Street--
I'm interested in maybe what the differences
might be-- a lot of people might be
familiar with AI in the context of software engineering
and the capabilities that are possible to accelerate software
engineering.
But I wonder if any of you could address the adoption
curve within finance.
What are different things that are in consideration.
As opposed to in a technology institution or organization,
what are different kinds of things that are being looked at
or that are important?
JEFF WECKER: So I'm happy to start and then
turn it over to my colleagues.
So we are mostly, at Two Sigma technology firm that invests,
of the 1800s employees that we have,
about just under 1,000 are in engineering.
Another 400 or 500 are modeling.
And then all the rest of the firm, the rest
do everything else.
So for most engineers, you give them a new tool--
and it's hard to believe.
You think about Claude being available in February of '25.
We started using it within a few weeks, and what GA,
within a month, six weeks.
So engineers, you see different rates of adoption,
but you see engineers ready to take
another tool in the toolbox, look at it,
and say, oh, I know how to build with it and start going.
What's exciting to me is the potential
to have everybody at the firm think of themselves as AI-first.
And there are different rates of adoption.
And it's becoming very clear, as we look at various metrics,
that those that adopt sooner or faster
are clearly becoming much more productive
by a lot of different measures that you look at,
code branches or work things they've
written, things they publish.
So our goal is to try to figure out
what is the right set of tools, what's
the right partnership for everyone at the firm
to be AI-first.
And while a lot of our focus at the firm
is on the investment pipeline, of course,
there's every single other workflow
at the firm that can lend itself to that.
We're seeing people now that have no technical backgrounds
are starting to use Claude in auto mode,
or one of our in-house workbenches in auto mode.
And it's really impressive to see people experiment.
And I think as a result, the rate of innovation
now is as high as it's been in recent memory.
BRADLEY OLSON: Fascinating.
ALI NAZARI: I guess I can add something to that.
The adoption is real.
In quantitative finance, Susquehanna particularly,
all engineers researchers are using AI tools.
As Jeff mentioned, there are different rate.
Some people use it more.
Some people use it less.
But one thing that is different in finance
compared to a software company is that the cost of mistakes.
So in a software company, if AI model make a mistake,
hopefully, you have unit tests.
You're going to figure it out.
You're going to fix it.
And you move on.
In finance, and many other fields, it can cost a lot.
It can cost money.
It can be kind of even a lot of other dangerous things
to the entire society in some cases.
So we need to be--
in general, quantitative finance has been an early adopter
of many, many things, whether it's statistical learning,
whether it's machine learning, different type of things.
But when it comes to agentic system, we need to be careful.
And then I would say that trust is something
that needs to be gained.
There are some things that I definitely use AI all the time
for, and there are some stuff that I
prefer human be part of it.
And then the other thing is that I think
trust needs to be regained.
Model change.
Data change.
Market change.
Market shift.
Everything happens.
And then something that you are trusting six months ago
might not be trustable right now.
So I think it's all about the mistake
and then the trust of the model.
BRADLEY OLSON: Jen, maybe one thing
I'd like to get your insight on is, how do you
encourage teams to experiment with and evaluate new AI tools
before deciding what to scale?
JEN ALLUM: I think an underappreciated quality
of firms like ours is that in many ways,
they operate like innovation businesses.
There's a relentless need to be able to innovate on what you do.
And that means the DNA is there for experimentation,
and history is there for experimentation.
DE Shaw is perhaps known as one of the original quant funds.
Of course, AI is in the DNA.
And as a federated business with multiple strategies,
we're able to unlock experiments across the organization
and allow for a bottoms up finding of where the value is.
So we think about the rate of learning
and the rate of discovery we have,
let lots of experiments run, be maximalist in the policy,
build and buy and everything in between,
and then see what catches fire.
And then think about where we scale that and for who and how.
So it's a continuous process that
is very much part of the DNA.
And this new advent of AI is accelerating.
BRADLEY OLSON: Li, I'd love to know in your organization,
how are you balancing the experimentation versus cost
problem that a lot of companies are facing right now.
LI DENG: Oh, yeah, very much so.
So compared with the high-tech world,
the quantum world has a similar kind of workflow.
You extract features.
That's what we call [? Ava. ?] And then you
have a model to do the forecast, just like prediction,
pattern recognition.
And then you do experimentation and evaluation.
We call it backtesting, whereas in high-tech world
you call the validation.
And then you go on testing in the high-tech world.
Now, we call paper trading or online trading.
Now, the key issue here is that the signals are extremely noisy.
The input signal is noisy.
The output signal is even more noisy.
So one of the reasons I actually decided
to move from Microsoft to go to the Wall Street
is I try to understand exactly.
I thought that the problem is going
to be unsupervised because the signal is so noisy,
you might as well just forget about the signal.
It turns out that it's a mix.
If you are purely using unsupervised learning,
you are not going to go anywhere.
And then you do have a little bit of supervision,
but it's extremely noisy-- the first time I look at the data,
financial data-- that's after visualizing all the returns--
I thought that I got a wrong data.
It's just random noise or random walk, almost everything there.
But it turned out that the signal is right.
You're able to extract very tiny bit of signal from there.
So we need to use a special kind of techniques, especially
in the experimentation and evaluation side.
So earlier on, we heard of Google DeepMind,
Oreo [? Vineyard. ?] He went through a recursive
self-improvement pipeline.
All this pipeline, we went through them all.
But we emphasized a lot more on the evaluation side.
And then because evaluation output is very, very noisy,
you don't even know what will be the right signal to predict,
and then how do you provide the right feedback in order
to further improve your features, et cetera.
So we put a lot of effort on that.
So the key over the past few years of the work upon AI,
it's not as much as making the model bigger.
You expect to have emergent capability coming out, just
like large language model.
We try quite a bit, but we don't know how far we are going to do.
But my hunch is that we need to go much further away because
of the nature of the noisy input/output [? line. ?]
So we actually gave up on that part.
And then the key focus would be, to your point,
how to make the entire system to form a right self-loop in such
a way that agentic method is really
the key that minimizes all the human effort,
engineer's effort, of an engineer's effort
to put them into place.
And that's the focus where we have to put in my current work.
JEFF WECKER: But if I could just add something
to the point about cost, because I think it's
going to play a growing role going forward.
If I think about historically our business, when
it was founded 26 years ago, most of our modeling
was fairly low dimensionality, statistical models
and then low-to-mid machine learning models.
And we moved from that to ensembles.
And we started to train our own transformers.
Then you had with GPT 3.5 coming out.
You Finally had the ability to use publicly available models
because the frontier firms gave you
such a head start in training.
That reduced the cost of doing that.
I think what we're seeing now with the advent of agent-centric
workflows, we are on the eve of potentially an explosive use
of compute demand that we have to be pretty careful
of because if--
I use the Two Sigma example.
We have 1,800 employees today.
But behind those 1,800 employees,
there are a quarter of a million agents doing operation,
all making their own compute demand that we really have
to think about the implications, return on investment of that.
Now, to be fair, when you're seeking alpha,
you dig a lot of dry wells.
There's no doubt about it.
But at some point, you have to look at the maturity
model of the investments that you're
making in identifying alpha opportunities,
and then think through whether or not
you're failing fast enough to protect
against the massive investment demand that you have in compute.
BRADLEY OLSON: Interesting.
I think maybe to switch gears there
because you mentioned the personnel.
One thing that is a great question for all organizations
is, how the AI age has changed the search for talent,
the recruiting process-- and would
love to hear from everyone about that--
and how the different things that you look for
has changed in this age and in this era.
Obviously, most people are looking for people of talent.
But how do you find them?
How do you sense that someone has a experimentation
capability and maybe the skills to make a lot out
of those things?
ALI NAZARI: I think-- yeah.
JEN ALLUM: We think about AI as an opportunity creator,
something that is helping us innovate and drive
higher quality work.
So we are deep in finding great talent continuously.
And DE Shaw, I think, is known in some ways
for hiring particular types of people and looks
for curiosity, lifelong learners, critical thinkers,
systems thinkers.
These are qualities that are becoming even more
important now.
And when people commit to the firm
and have decades long careers, as
is common, then actually all looking
for a degree of adaptability, that they
will have multiple careers within the organization.
So, as I'm building out a team and I'm
thinking about how to hire, it's emphasizing those qualities more
alongside functional expertise, and then building on that,
thinking ahead to what's the next role and the role
after that they'll be doing with us.
ALI NAZARI: Yeah, I completely agree.
And then I think some of the qualities
still is going to stay the same.
So we want smart people that who are curious,
who are asking the right questions, who
can work independently.
And then these qualities matters actually maybe more than before.
One thing that changed, though, is that the interview process.
The type of thing that you were questioning people
before was built for a time that implementation was the hardest
part.
Now that AI does a good amount of implementation
for us, the type of things that we care about change as well.
We need to make sure that people can adopt this kind of thing.
They can use the tools properly.
And they can detect if an AI system like, confidently
wrong about something, they should be able to detect it.
One thing I'm actually wondering is that the next generation,
how are they going to develop judgment.
If you think about judgment, traditionally,
what we were doing is that we try something.
We make a mistake.
We learn from that mistake.
And then how judgment is being developed.
Now that AI does most of the experimentation for us,
the question is how that judgment
is going to be developed.
And this is the question, I guess, for next generation.
LI DENG: Yeah.
So in my firm, for example, maybe just two years ago,
most of the team members are PhDs from Ivy League
from mathematics, from physics, some computer science.
Nowadays, I think 2/3 of them are no longer with the firm.
Before, sometime, every now and then,
we get the CV coming from universities.
They don't even have PhD.
We don't even look at the CV to say, sorry,
we don't hire non-PhD.
But now we have maybe more than half
of the people who are not even PhD.
For the intern, we actually enjoy
senior undergraduate students to didn't come.
They actually can do agentic work probably faster than
full-time--
the people there.
So all the talents-- actually, profile changed quite a bit
just over the past two years.
JEFF WECKER: Yeah, if I could just clear something up,
we are hiring.
We are hiring.
But I do think what people are doing is very different.
We've eliminated coding tests, of course,
because we'd be testing LLMs and not people.
But I do think that the kind of scientists, the kind of computer
scientists, the kind of engineer is going to be even more
important to us going forward.
Their ability to take a problem, decompose
problems clearly into components--
can they actually prompt to get the kinds of outcomes
that we really want to see?
Can they design agents that are able to use judgment and really
help to accelerate either the generation of features,
the generation of models, the generation of order placement
or portfolio construction models.
That's going to be critical.
So we're looking for people that have the cognitive depth
to be inquisitive and learn our business
and then bring to-- bear the skills that they've learned
in their various scientific backgrounds,
to apply them to deconstruct the ideas that they may have
about what's possible in the future,
and then deliver outcomes.
BRADLEY OLSON: Well, I think it's certainly
good for everyone in this room to know that people are hiring,
that it's possible out there.
I think another thing that I'd like
to ask that I think is relevant to the talent question,
for those of you who are willing to answer,
is, if you were going to design a quant firm from scratch,
what might be different about it now?
In this age, what might you do differently
than maybe the existing systems and infrastructure
that you've seen?
ALI NAZARI: So I think one thing that I would do is that--
I think quantitative trading has two parts.
One is the research side.
The other one is trading.
One side is creating the knowledge.
The other side is using the knowledge.
So, if I want to build a new quantitative trading firms,
I basically focus more and more on the research side.
And there are a couple of things I'm
going to do on research side.
The first thing I'm going to do, make sure
that every single experiment, the failures, the successes,
everything that has been done has
become part of the knowledge of the organization.
I guess there are things that--
especially the failures.
Many people put them in their mind.
And then when they leave the company,
the knowledge goes with them.
The second thing I would do is that making sure
that the evaluation becomes part of the research loop,
not something that we add at the end.
And the third thing I'm going to do essentially
is going to be making sure that researchers,
the human research and AI researchers,
go to the same kind of research process.
They're going to be evaluated the same way regardless
of whether is AI-generated or human-generated.
And then the knowledge we're going to learn from both of them
is going to go to the knowledge of the entire organization.
I look at research as not a collection of task.
Is it process of continuous learning?
And I think that's the big distinction.
JEN ALLUM: While we build a fair amount at DE Shaw,
we also partner widely with companies outside
and like to be a good partner in terms of collaboration,
especially when you think about enterprise readiness for what
it takes to be able to deliver a product in a regulated space
where we care about security and care about our IP deeply.
And when we look at products, I think to Ali's point
about the kind of know how the organizations already
have both technically and knowledge wise,
I think there is an opportunity for even sharper thinking
about the value proposition of new products
in this space, about what they would be,
how they would be additive to companies like these.
BRADLEY OLSON: Well, I have a bit of a wild card question.
I want to see if people are up for answering.
But I think I'd love to hear what so many people think
about this question.
If you're not up for answering, we can go to another one.
But I'd love to know, if anyone wants to weigh in,
what is one widely held belief about AI that you
think is wrong?
JEFF WECKER: I think the idea that you need fewer people.
Certainly, there are roles in jobs that are not
going to exist in the future.
But the idea that you don't need technologists, scientists,
mathematicians in a world where more systemic decision
support is going to be the future,
I think it will turn out to be false.
Now, I believe what will happen as a result is
a whole host of new roles are going
to be generated to take up the changes that are going on
in the workforce.
But I do believe that one of the ideas that are being advocated
is that there won't be opportunities
for people in the future.
It just doesn't make a lot of sense.
It hasn't been true with any other major invention
over human history.
The world's changed.
The markets grow.
And the opportunity for more people to make an impact
continues to grow.
BRADLEY OLSON: Does anyone else want to try that one?
Yeah.
ALI NAZARI: I guess I can.
LI DENG: Go ahead.
ALI NAZARI: Go ahead.
LI DENG: Yeah, so we heard earlier talk
several talks in robotics and also in foundational model
people still talk about one wave of scaling
and the second wave of scaling.
There could be third wave scaling.
So I personally feel that maybe it could--
I think for robotics, it could be true,
whereas in finance, I just don't believe
this is going to be correct.
We have done a lot of work over the past few years trying
to scale.
We never reached the point where we have the emerging
capability come up.
But I think in finance, the most important part really
is the systematic way of looking at the full system, especially
the integration between different components of machine
learning, especially at the output side, evaluation
and the feedback because feedback in the financial market
is a very, very different type of problem
than in the high-tech.
And that part of design probably carries a lot more weight
in the agentic area.
And I remember, when I moved from Microsoft to Citadel
seven years ago, my big boss, very wealthy, billionaire,
he actually first personally told me that, I will hire you.
We know that you disrupt the speech recognition.
You practically solve speech recognition problem,
and then you do natural.
We hire you.
It's not-- we don't expect you to bring that kind of expertise
to Citadel, because if you build a system for translation system,
for recognition system, it may work today.
And then more likely next week, you don't have to adapt.
Maybe when you wait for three or four
years, when you have different president,
for example, the language change.
And then you have one president, different policy, different--
And then language model change that
will affect speech recognition.
At that time, you have to adapt.
And maybe for voice, you might want--
you have to wait maybe a few years when
coding standard changes.
Maybe whatever system that you trained before may not
may break.
If you want to bring that kind of system into financial world,
you're going to fail because in financial market, every time
you put order into the market, people react that differently.
It changes the environment much more so
than the high-tech world.
I think this is the drastic difference
between different world.
So I think a traditional way of thinking
in high-tech world of scaling and then
doing all sorts of things that you heard here,
maybe most of them may not be applicable to us.
BRADLEY OLSON: Well, thank you all for joining
and thank you for hearing and listening to us.
I think that concludes our panel today.
And yeah, thanks, everyone, for listening.
JEFF WECKER: Thank you.
LI DENG: Thank you.
[APPLAUSE]
